en: The *Dharmasāgara-sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Campā, staying on the banks of Lake Haṃsakalāpī, together with a great [assembly].
The assembly of bhikṣus was gathered together.
On the fifteenth day of the month, it was time for the recitation of the precepts.
The Buddha sat, and after the assembly had been convened for some time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not recite the precepts.
The attendant Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt, and addressed the Buddha:

"The first watch of the night has passed and the middle watch is approaching; the great assembly has gathered for a long time. I fear that the World-Honored One may be weary; I pray that you will preach the precepts at this time."
The Buddha remained silent.
After the assembly had sat for a long time, there was a bhikṣu named Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya who adjusted his robes, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha:

"The first watch and the middle watch of the night have passed, and the roosters are about to crow. May the World-Honored One not be weary; as the community of monks has gathered for a long time, we pray that the Buddha will recite the precepts."
The World-Honored One remained silent once more.
Again, he addressed him, saying:
"The morning star has already risen; the time is passing."
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! Listen: because there is one who is impure among the Saṃgha, I am unable to recite the precepts."
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I shall concentrate my mind to observe who among them is impure.
Maudgalyāyana then addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to concentrate my mind and observe who among you is impure; let that impure one depart from the assembly.
The World-Honored One said, "Your desire to concentrate your mind and observe the impure one so as to have him leave the assembly is most excellent; you may do so."
Maudgalyāyana immediately entered meditative concentration to observe the situation and saw that his disciple had violated a grave precept.
Rising from his concentration, he went before the bhikṣu who had broken the precept and rebuked him, saying:
"You have become a śramaṇa; the observance of the precepts is your foundation. The precepts are like the head of a person."
The śramaṇa’s conduct of precepts ought to be pure and white, like water or jade.

This is the seat of the Tathāgata, the assembly of the worthy and holy, the gathering of those who transcend the world, and the place where those of pure morality congregate. This seat is like a grove of sandalwood, yet you, with your foul and putrid *elā* wood, have defiled its true essence.
Maudgalyāyana took his disciple by the hand and led him out, saying, "You are a person who has been cast aside;
you may not participate in the pure assembly of the Tathāgata’s great multitude."

"Do not allow those who are defiled and turbid to join this great assembly of the Great Sangha. Just as the great ocean does not accept a foul corpse, you must reflect upon this yourself and do not defile the assembly of the virtuous.
Once the defiled person had departed, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The defiled and turbid person has already been cast far away; the assembly is now pure. We only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the precepts at the proper time."
The World-Honored One remained silent once more.
Maudgalyāyana, finding this strange, looked in all four directions and saw that the bhikṣu who had just left was already back in his seat. Maudgalyāyana addressed him again, saying:
"You are a person who has cast himself out; why do you not withdraw from your own sinful defilements and yet sit heavily upon this seat once more?"
Maudgalyāyana sent him away again, whereupon he rose from his seat and departed.
Maudgalyāyana spoke once more to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One!"

"The defiled persons have already departed and the great assembly is now pure; there are no longer any who are corrupt or evil. We only pray that the World-Honored One will proclaim the precepts at this time, so that the Sangha may cultivate pure deeds."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer recite the precepts; you yourselves may recite them together. Whether it be I who recite the precepts,"

If a person among the assembly violates the precepts yet remains silent and does not acknowledge their own transgression, while still taking a seat like that of the Tathāgata, this constitutes silent lying.
For silent lying, one's head shall split into seven pieces.
“The Tathāgata preaching the precepts to the great assembly is extremely difficult; from this day forward, you shall recite the precepts yourselves.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha:
“When a disciple hears the Way, it is the Tathāgata who first transforms them; it is not that the disciple attains the Way through their own self-awakening.”
The sublime virtue of the Tathāgata is as profound and vast as heaven and earth; his words are true and essential. When disciples recite and practice them, they attain the fruit of the Way.
The Tathāgata is like the rain from heaven: among the hundred grains, grasses, and trees, there is none that does not look up to him for its flourishing.
Yet the disciples' virtue is shallow and their realization small, so people do not submit to or believe them.
"The World-Honored One takes pity on the ignorant masses, enabling all to attain peace, gain faith and the right path, and fulfill their aspirations.
Maudgalyāyana made this earnest and persistent request three, four, and even five times.
The World-Honored One told Maudgalyāyana:
"For the sake of all, you have entreated the Tathāgata with such earnestness, even up to four or five times; I shall now speak it for you all."
My monastic Dharma is like the great ocean, possessing eight virtues; you all should listen to them.
The waters of the great ocean are neither overfull nor deficient;
my Dharma is likewise, being neither overfull nor deficient—this is its first virtue.
The tides of the great ocean arrive at their appointed times and never fail to reach their proper places;
likewise, those among my fourfold assembly who receive my precepts do not violate the prohibitions or deviate from the constant Dharma—this is the second virtue.
The waters of the great ocean have but a single flavor; they possess no manifold flavors, for there is nothing that does not have salt as its taste. My Dharma is likewise:

the flavor of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) consists in the resolve to seek tranquility, thereby bringing about supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the flavor of the Four Noble Truths consists in the resolve to seek the four paths, thereby unraveling the bonds of affliction; the flavor of the Mahāyāna consists in the resolve to seek the Great Vow, thereby delivering all sentient beings. This is the third virtue.
The great ocean is both deep and vast, such that nothing can limit it;

the Dharma of the Sangha is likewise, being profoundly subtle in every respect. Among all things great in the eight directions, none is greater than the Dharma of the Sangha; the Dharma of the Sangha is the most expansive and magnificent—this is its fourth virtue.
Within the great ocean, there is nothing that is not fully present—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, musaragalva, agate, and the wondrous maṇi jewels;

likewise, within my Saṃgha’s Dharma, there is nothing that is not fully present among the wondrous treasures of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: the divine feet for dwelling in long life, the power to soar through the ten directions reaching everywhere without exception, and the ability to traverse immeasurable Buddha-fields in a mere instant, arriving at most excellent lands and using those paths to transform and guide all living beings while purifying one's own Buddha-land. This is the fifth virtue.

Within the great ocean dwell divine dragons, such as the Dragon King Sāgara, Anavatapta, Nanda, Upananda, and Airāvata. These dragons possess immeasurable and sublime virtue; they are capable of creating celestial palaces, and there are no species of creatures that do not look up to them in reliance. My Saṃgha is likewise so:

the four pairs and eight ranks of noble ones, the twelve worthy ones, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—their merit in teaching and transforming others flourishes ever more and becomes ever more beautiful. This is the sixth virtue.

The great ocean receives and contains the hundreds of rivers and myriad streams; the waters of the Ganges and Indus are all received by it, yet throughout day and night, it bears no name of overflowing or depletion.

My Sangha’s Dharma is likewise: whether those of the lineage of Brahmā or Śakra enter the Sangha’s Dharma, or those of the four castes of noble repute—whether Śākya or Brahmā, or of royal descent who have abandoned worldly nobility to enter our true transformation, or even craftsmen of humble birth who likewise enter our true transformation—though their lineages differ, once they have donned the robes and practiced the Great Way, they become of one single flavor. There are none who are not sons of the Śākya; this is the seventh virtue.
The great ocean is pure; it does not accept corpses and is free from all filth and turbidity, receiving only that which belongs to the sea itself.

My Sangha’s Dharma is likewise pure, like the great ocean: it does not accept the foul and evil. Those who violate the precepts and prohibitions, those who are not practitioners of pure *brahmacarya*, may not be received at all; they are cast out and distanced, just as the ocean does not accept corpses. This is the eighth virtue.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

“The great assembly of the Tathāgata is purely virtuous; because there are those whose conduct regarding the prohibitions and precepts is not pure and who are not of the Śākya lineage, I do not recite the precepts for them.”
"You, sirs, must well admonish and instruct one another so that the True Dharma shall not be corrupted.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. *Dharmasāgara-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Ocean of Dharma).
